---
title: "Synthetic Age-at-Death Mixture"
description: "A bounded two-component distribution created for mathematical exploration"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("../R/diagnostics.R")
source("../R/simulation.R")
source("../R/plots.R")
source("../R/extensions.R")
source("../R/extension_plots.R")
library(ggplot2)
bands <- read.csv("../results/calibration_bands.csv")
population <- make_age_population()
all_results <- read.csv("../results/extension_diagnostics.csv")
page_results <- all_results[all_results$case_id == "age_mixture", ]
simulation <- simulate_population(population, B = 10000L, seed = 631L, keep_means = TRUE)
selected_n <- c(5, 75, 200)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Synthetic distribution"}
This graph-inspired population is not fitted historical mortality data. It is used only to study how averaging acts on a bounded, irregular, two-component distribution.
:::

## 1. Question and role

How quickly does an average become approximately Normal when the parent distribution has a sharp early component, a broad later component, and a deep valley between them?

## 2. Population construction

For integer support from 0 through 100, the instructor construction uses

$$
w_E(x)=0.045e^{-x/5}.
$$

$$
w_A(x)=0.030\exp\left[-\frac12\left(\frac{x-65}{10}\right)^2\right].
$$

then normalizes $w_E(x)+w_A(x)$ to sum to one.

```{r}
#| label: fig-age-components
#| fig-cap: "The synthetic population combines a rapidly decreasing early component with a broad component centered near 65. The normalized curve is a mathematical construction, not an empirical life table."
#| fig-alt: "Three curves showing an early spike, a later bell-shaped component, and their normalized combination."
plot_age_components(population$distribution)
```

## 3. Theory and prediction

Exact weighted sums give mean `r sprintf("%.2f", population$mean)` and SD `r sprintf("%.2f", sqrt(population$variance))`. The observations are iid, bounded, and finite-variance, so the ordinary CLT applies. I expected the bimodal parent to leave visible asymmetry at small $n$, then converge faster than the unbounded Exponential case.

## 4. Simulation design

The grid runs from $n=1$ through 300 with extra attention near 75. Every point uses 10,000 repeated samples and seed 631. The same calibrated evidence categories used for the required populations are retained.

## 5. Numerical evidence

```{r}
#| label: tbl-age-diagnostics
#| tbl-cap: "The synthetic mixture reaches small skewness near n = 75. Q-Q RMSE sits near the strict Normal-noise band and fluctuates slightly afterward."
shown <- page_results[page_results$n %in% c(30, 50, 75, 100, 150, 200), c("n", "mean_error", "relative_se_error", "skewness", "excess_kurtosis", "qq_rmse")]
names(shown) <- c("n", "Center error", "Relative SE error", "Skewness", "Excess kurtosis", "Q-Q RMSE")
knitr::kable(shown, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
```

## 6. Sampling-distribution evidence

```{r}
#| label: fig-age-sampling
#| fig-cap: "At n = 5 the parent mixture still leaves asymmetry. By n = 75 and 200 the averages closely follow the dark theoretical Normal overlays. Each panel uses its own horizontal scale so the narrowing distributions remain assessable."
#| fig-alt: "Three histograms on separately labeled horizontal scales, progressing from asymmetric at five observations to nearly bell-shaped at larger sample sizes."
plot_sampling_distributions(simulation$means, population, selected_n, facet_scales = "free")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-age-qq
#| fig-cap: "Q-Q curvature is material at n = 5 and small by n = 75. The remaining endpoint movement is minor compared with the parent population's irregular shape."
#| fig-alt: "Three Q-Q panels that straighten substantially as sample size rises."
plot_qq_comparison(simulation$means, population, selected_n)
```

## 7. Diagnostic trajectory and SE

```{r}
#| label: fig-age-trajectory
#| fig-cap: "Shape diagnostics fall rapidly through n = 75. Small later reversals in Q-Q RMSE are finite-simulation variation, not evidence that convergence reverses."
#| fig-alt: "Three log-scale trajectory panels with declining shape diagnostics."
plot_diagnostic_trajectory(simulation$summary, population, bands)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-age-se
#| fig-cap: "Empirical and theoretical standard errors nearly overlap across the grid, confirming the exact weighted variance calculation."
#| fig-alt: "Two nearly overlapping standard-error curves decreasing with sample size."
plot_se_comparison(simulation$summary, population)
```

## 8. Decision and disagreement

**Decision: $n=75$ is the smallest defensible tested value.** Skewness is about `r sprintf("%.3f", page_results$skewness[page_results$n == 75])`, the histogram and Q-Q plot are convincing, and the conclusion remains visually stable at 100 and 150. Q-Q RMSE moves just above the calibration band at some larger points; that small fluctuation is retained as Monte Carlo disagreement rather than interpreted as reversed convergence.

## 9. Limitation and surprise

The numerical result belongs only to this constructed probability vector. It says nothing about any population, place, or historical period. The surprise is how completely averaging can conceal a parent with two visibly separate components.

## 10. Conclusion

A bounded but highly irregular parent can yield a useful Normal approximation by about 75 observations. Parent multimodality alone does not prevent the ordinary CLT.
